1. Plain settings: `Bind` + `ValidateOnStart`.
2. Rules over those settings: `IValidateOptions<T>`.
3. Values derived from settings or registrations: `PostConfigure`.
4. Behavior (not data) built from multiple options: a dedicated service injecting `IOptions<T>`.

---

# Observability

---

## Metrics Conventions

Metrics use `System.Diagnostics.Metrics` with one meter per domain, exported through OpenTelemetry to Prometheus.

## Telemetry class per domain

Each domain has a static `Telemetry` class with an `internal static readonly Meter` named `YourApp.<Domain>` and `internal static readonly` instruments.

```csharp
internal static class Telemetry
{
    internal static readonly Meter Meter = new("YourApp.Download");

    internal static readonly Counter<long> Completed =
        Meter.CreateCounter<long>("yourapp.download.completed_total");

    internal static readonly Counter<long> Failed =
        Meter.CreateCounter<long>("yourapp.download.failed_total");

    internal static readonly Histogram<double> Duration =
        Meter.CreateHistogram<double>("yourapp.download.duration_seconds", unit: "s");

    private static int _queueSize;

    internal static readonly ObservableGauge<int> QueueSize =
        Meter.CreateObservableGauge("yourapp.download.queue_size", () => _queueSize);

    internal static void SetQueueSize(int value) => _queueSize = value;
}
```

:::note[No abstraction]
No base class, no shared `IMetrics` wrapper, no generic helper for meters. Each domain's `Telemetry` class is plain static code.
:::


## Registration

Register every meter centrally in the telemetry setup, then export with Prometheus.

```csharp
services.AddOpenTelemetry()
    .WithMetrics(m => m
        .AddMeter("YourApp.Download")
        .AddMeter("YourApp.Search")
        .AddPrometheusExporter());
```

A meter that is not registered emits nothing, so add the `.AddMeter(...)` line in the same change that creates the meter.

## Naming

| Element | Rule | Example |
|---------|------|---------|
| Meter | `YourApp.<Domain>` | `YourApp.Download` |
| Instrument | `yourapp.<domain>.<metric_name>` in snake_case | `yourapp.download.duration_seconds` |
| Counter | ends with `_total` | `yourapp.search.requests_total` |
| Time histogram | ends with `_seconds` | `yourapp.search.duration_seconds` |

## Tags

- Short, lowercase names: `reason`, `source`, `type`, `status`, `phase`.
- Cardinality must stay bounded.

:::danger[Never use unbounded values as tags]
Entity IDs, file names, URLs, and query strings create one time series per value and will overwhelm the metrics backend. Map them to a small fixed set (`reason=timeout`) instead.
:::


```csharp
Telemetry.Failed.Add(1, new KeyValuePair<string, object?>("reason", "timeout"));
```

## ObservableGauge

Use a static backing field with an `internal static void Set*()` setter. The actor (or service) calls the setter when the value changes. The gauge callback only reads the field.

This keeps the gauge callback free of actor state access and thread-safety concerns.

## Instrument at the operation boundary

Record metrics where the operation completes, success or failure, not at each call site that starts it.

```csharp
// Good: one place, covers every path
private void Complete(Stopwatch sw, bool ok)
{
    Telemetry.Duration.Record(sw.Elapsed.TotalSeconds);
    (ok ? Telemetry.Completed : Telemetry.Failed).Add(1);
}
```

This prevents double counting and missed failure paths when an operation has several entry points.

---

## Logging Conventions

Which logger you use depends on where the code runs. Structured templates are mandatory everywhere.

## Which logger

| Context | Logger |
|---------|--------|
| Akka actors | `ILoggingAdapter` via `Context.GetLogger()` |
| Services, endpoints, hosted services | `ILogger<T>` from Microsoft.Extensions.Logging |

:::danger[No ILogger in actors]
Never inject or use `ILogger` inside an actor. Use the Akka `ILoggingAdapter` so log events carry actor path and flow through the actor system's logging pipeline.
:::


```csharp
public sealed class DownloadWorker : ReceiveActor
{
    private readonly ILoggingAdapter _log = Context.GetLogger();

    public DownloadWorker()
    {
        Receive<StartDownload>(cmd =>
            _log.Info("Starting download {DownloadId}", cmd.DownloadId));
    }
}

public sealed class RuleSetLoader(ILogger<RuleSetLoader> logger)
{
    public void Load(string id) =>
        logger.LogInformation("Loading ruleset {RuleSetId}", id);
}
```

## Structured templates

Use message templates with named placeholders. Never use string interpolation or concatenation in log calls.

```csharp
_log.Warning("Retry {Attempt} for {DownloadId}", attempt, id);   // correct
_log.Warning($"Retry {attempt} for {id}");                        // wrong
```

Interpolation destroys structure (no queryable properties) and allocates even when the level is disabled.

## Thread-safety restrictions

:::caution[Never log inside PipeTo callbacks]
`PipeTo` success/failure delegates run outside the actor's message-processing context. Return a message instead and log in the handler that receives it.
:::


:::caution[Never use `Context.GetLogger()` inside Akka.Streams lambdas]
Stream stages run on a different thread, and `Context` is not valid there. Capture the `ILoggingAdapter` into a local variable before building the stream, or log from the actor when the stream completes.
:::


```csharp
var log = _log; // captured on the actor thread
Source.From(items)
    .Select(i => { log.Debug("Processing {Item}", i); return i; });
```

## Log levels

| Level | Use for |
|-------|---------|
| Debug | Flow tracing, state transitions, per-message detail |
| Information | Business events (download completed, ruleset loaded) |
| Warning | Recoverable issues (retry, fallback, rejected input) |
| Error | Failures that need attention |

Pass the exception as the first argument rather than formatting its message into the template.

```csharp
_log.Error(ex, "Download {DownloadId} failed", id);
logger.LogError(ex, "Download {DownloadId} failed", id);
```

## Sink configuration

Serilog is the sink, configured once in the host. Domain projects reference only the abstractions (`ILogger<T>`, `ILoggingAdapter`) and never configure sinks, enrichers, or minimum levels themselves.

Minimum levels and overrides belong in `appsettings.json` so they can change per environment without a rebuild.

## Do not log

- Secrets, tokens, API keys, and passwords.
- Full request or response bodies at Information level.
- Personal data without a documented reason.

---

# CI/CD

---

## Build Pipeline

The build has one job: prove the solution compiles cleanly, is formatted, and passes its tests. All commands run from the repository root.

The template repositories ([dotnet.application](https://github.com/st0o0/dotnet.application), [dotnet.library](https://github.com/st0o0/dotnet.library)) ship with CI workflows that run these steps automatically. See [GitHub Actions](github-actions) for the workflow setup.

## Steps

```powershell
dotnet build src/YourApp.slnx
dotnet format src/YourApp.slnx --verify-no-changes
dotnet run --project src/YourApp.Search.Tests/YourApp.Search.Tests.csproj
```

1. `dotnet build` compiles every project.
2. `dotnet format --verify-no-changes` fails when any file deviates from `.editorconfig`.
3. Tests run per test project.

Run `dotnet format` locally after editing `.cs` files so CI does not reject the change.

## Zero warnings

Set `TreatWarningsAsErrors` once in `Directory.Build.props`:

```xml
<Project>
  <PropertyGroup>
    <TreatWarningsAsErrors>true</TreatWarningsAsErrors>
  </PropertyGroup>
</Project>
```

:::danger[Never add NoWarn]
The build must stay at 0 warnings. Fix the cause. Do not add `<NoWarn>`, `#pragma warning disable`, or `.editorconfig` severity downgrades to make a warning go away.
:::


Warnings as errors also gives you compile-time guarantees for patterns like exhaustive `switch` expressions (a missing arm is CS8509).

## Tests: dotnet run, not dotnet test

xUnit v3 test projects are executables on Microsoft.Testing.Platform. Run them with `dotnet run`.

```powershell
dotnet run --project src/YourApp.Download.Tests/YourApp.Download.Tests.csproj
```

:::note
`dotnet test` is the VSTest entry point and is not the supported path for xUnit v3 on Microsoft.Testing.Platform. Pass extra options after `--`, for example `-- --report-trx`.
:::


In test code, pass `TestContext.Current.CancellationToken` to every call that accepts a `CancellationToken` (analyzer xUnit1051). The code fix can apply this:

```powershell
dotnet format analyzers src/YourApp.slnx --diagnostics xUnit1051 --severity info
```

## Coverage and quality gate

| Signal | Role |
|--------|------|
| Code coverage | Collected and reported, **not a gate** |
| Mutation testing | **The quality gate** |

Coverage only shows which lines ran. Mutation testing shows whether the tests would notice a change in behavior. Do not set a minimum coverage threshold that fails the build, because it rewards assertion-free tests.

See [GitHub Actions](github-actions) for how mutation testing is scheduled.

## Checklist

- [x] Build and format run from the repo root
- [x] `TreatWarningsAsErrors` in `Directory.Build.props`
- [x] No `NoWarn` anywhere
- [x] Tests run with `dotnet run`
- [x] Coverage collected, mutation score is the gate

---

## GitHub Actions

Workflows are split by cost: fast checks on every change, slow checks on a schedule. All CI workflows call reusable workflows from [github-workflows](https://github.com/st0o0/github-workflows) - pin to a major version tag (e.g. `@v1`).

The template repositories ([dotnet.application](https://github.com/st0o0/dotnet.application), [dotnet.library](https://github.com/st0o0/dotnet.library)) ship with these workflows pre-configured. You should not need to write them from scratch.

## Reusable workflows

| Workflow | Purpose |
|----------|---------|
| `dotnet-ci.yml` | Build, test, security (Trivy and CodeQL) |
| `dotnet-release-docker.yml` | Per-RID publish, multi-arch Docker, cosign signing |
| `dotnet-release-nuget.yml` | Build, test, pack, NuGet push, GitHub Release asset |
| `dotnet-dev-build.yml` | Label-gated PR dev image (per-RID, multi-arch) |
| `commitlint.yml` | Commit message validation via Conventional Commits |
| `security.yml` | Trivy Docker image scan with SARIF upload |
| `labeler.yml` | Path-based PR labeling |
| `labels.yml` | Label definition sync |

## CI workflow

Runs build, format check, and tests on every push and pull request.

```yaml
name: ci
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  ci:
    uses: st0o0/github-workflows/.github/workflows/dotnet-ci.yml@v1
    with:
      solution-file: src/ProjectName.slnx
```

The `dotnet-ci` workflow reads the SDK version from `global.json` so CI and local development use the same SDK. See [Build Pipeline](build) for the commands themselves.

## Release architecture

Use release-please to create releases from Conventional Commits, then chain build and publish jobs.

```yaml
name: release
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

permissions:
  contents: write
  packages: write
  id-token: write

jobs:
  release-please:
    uses: st0o0/github-workflows/.github/workflows/release-please.yml@v1

  docker:
    needs: release-please
    if: needs.release-please.outputs.release_created == 'true'
    uses: st0o0/github-workflows/.github/workflows/dotnet-release-docker.yml@v1
    with:
      version: ${{ needs.release-please.outputs.version }}
      image-name: projectname
      image-description: "Project description"
```

For NuGet libraries, replace the docker job with `dotnet-release-nuget.yml`:

```yaml
  nuget:
    needs: release-please
    if: needs.release-please.outputs.release_created == 'true'
    uses: st0o0/github-workflows/.github/workflows/dotnet-release-nuget.yml@v1
    with:
      version: ${{ needs.release-please.outputs.version }}
      solution-file: src/ProjectName.slnx
      publish-project: src/ProjectName/ProjectName.csproj
      package-name: ProjectName
    secrets:
      NUGET_USER: ${{ secrets.NUGET_USER }}
```

:::tip
The release workflow runs release-please first, then only chains build/publish when `release_created` is true. This avoids the GITHUB_TOKEN limitation where workflow-created releases do not trigger `on: release`.
:::

## Mutation testing

:::caution[Schedule it, do not run it on PRs]
Mutation testing is too slow for pull requests. Run it weekly on a schedule and allow manual dispatch.
:::

Use a matrix with one job per target project so jobs run in parallel and one failing target does not hide the others.

```yaml
name: mutation
on:
  schedule:
    - cron: "0 3 * * 0"
  workflow_dispatch:

jobs:
  mutate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        target: [Search, Download, Scoring, Feed]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-dotnet@v4
        with:
          global-json-file: global.json
      - run: dotnet tool restore
      - run: dotnet stryker --config-file src/ProjectName.${{ matrix.target }}.Tests/stryker-config.json
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: mutation-${{ matrix.target }}
          path: "**/StrykerOutput/**/reports/*"
```

## Security scanning

The `security.yml` workflow scans Docker images with Trivy and uploads results to the GitHub Security tab.

```yaml
  security:
    uses: st0o0/github-workflows/.github/workflows/security.yml@v1
    with:
      docker-image-name: projectname
```

## Docker image build (PR dev builds)

Label-gated dev image builds on PRs, useful for testing changes in a staging environment.

```yaml
  dev-build:
    uses: st0o0/github-workflows/.github/workflows/dotnet-dev-build.yml@v1
    with:
      image-name: projectname
```

## Do not push results to the repo

:::danger
Never commit test results, coverage reports, or mutation reports back to the repository from a workflow. They create noisy history and merge conflicts.
:::

Upload them as workflow artifacts (`actions/upload-artifact`) or publish to a report site instead.

## Permissions

The calling job must declare its own `permissions:` block. Without it, the reusable workflow run fails with `Invalid workflow file`.

## Checklist

- [x] CI on every push and PR via `dotnet-ci.yml`
- [x] Releases via release-please + chained build/publish
- [x] Commit messages enforced via `commitlint.yml`
- [x] Mutation testing weekly, matrix per target
- [x] Security scanning via `security.yml`
- [x] Reports as artifacts, never committed
- [x] All workflows pinned to `@v1` from [github-workflows](https://github.com/st0o0/github-workflows)
